method: A specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one kelvin, an intensive material property measured in joules per kilogram-kelvin. Every listed unit is reduced to that SI base by one exact factor. The joule per kilogram-kelvin and the joule per kilogram-degree Celsius carry the same factor, because a temperature interval of one kelvin is one degree Celsius, and the kilojoule is 1000 joules. The calorie units follow NIST Special Publication 811 Table B.8: the International Table calorie is exactly 4.1868 J and the thermochemical calorie exactly 4.184 J, so cal_IT/(g·°C) is 4186.8 J/(kg·K) and cal_th/(g·°C) is 4184 J/(kg·K). The Btu units use the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, a pound of 0.45359237 kg and a temperature interval of 5/9 K per degree Fahrenheit, which makes Btu_IT/(lb·°F) exactly 4186.8 J/(kg·K) — the well-known equality with the International Table calorie per gram — while Btu_th/(lb·°F) is 4184 J/(kg·K). A kilowatt-hour is exactly 3.6 MJ. A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, an exponent form is refused, and values that are zero, negative or above 100,000,000 J/(kg·K) are rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped. The reference table holds round capacities in four systems for checking a conversion, and the output also states the joules one kilogram takes for one kelvin, which equals the base value. Temperature-dependent capacities are not tabulated and no material is recommended. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), Table B.8 Specific Heat Capacity and Specific Entropy: cal_IT/(g·°C) and Btu_IT/(lb·°F) are 4.1868 × 10^3 J/(kg·K), the thermochemical values 4.184 × 10^3 J/(kg·K)
